Abstract 
The effect of smoking using liquid smoke flavourings on the hydrolysis and 
oxidation of European sea bass lipids during in vitro digestion was investigated. The 
techniques used were 1H NMR and SPME-GC/MS. The former proved that liquid 
smoking does not influence the extent of lipolysis, but prevents those lipid oxidation 
reactions that occur during in vitro digestion of unsmoked samples, giving rise to 
cis,trans-conjugated dienes associated with hydroperoxy/hydroxy groups. SPME-
GC/MS corroborated the results obtained by 1H NMR in relation to the antioxidant 
effect of smoking under gastrointestinal conditions. Smoked sea bass digests showed 
lower abundances of volatile oxidation markers derived from omega-3 and omega-6 
lipids than unsmoked ones. Moreover, the lowest values were found in the digests of sea 
bass samples smoked with the flavouring showing the highest phenolic content. For the 
first time, the bioaccessibility of smoke flavouring components was evidenced, some of 
them well-known for displaying antioxidant activity.

1. Introduction 
Fish shelf-life during storage is rather limited by microbiological spoilage 
and by its great susceptibility to oxidation of its polyunsaturated omega-3 lipids. 
To avoid these problems, different preservation techniques, such as smoking, 
have been applied to fish from ancient times up to the present day. In recent 
decades the use of commercial smoke flavourings, i.e. complex mixtures of 
smoke components retained in a liquid or solid carrier, instead of traditional 
smoking techniques using burning or smoldering materials has increased because 
of its many advantages. Among these can be cited: ease of application and a 
better control not only of sensory characteristics of smoked products, but also of 
the presence of smoke-derived toxic compounds, such as polycyclic aromatic 
hydrocarbons (Guillén & Ibargoitia, 1998).  
The extension of fish shelf-life and oxidative stability due to the smoking 
process has been addressed in previous studies, in which special attention was 
paid to the effect of different smoke flavouring compositions and application 
methods (Alcicek, 2011; Vidal, Goicoechea, Manzanos, & Guillén, 2016a; Vidal, 
Manzanos, Goicoechea, & Guillén, 2016b). Nevertheless, the effect of smoked 
fish during human digestion still remains unknown. It could be expected that the 
well-known beneficial effects of the smoke components during fish meat storage, 
would also occur in vivo during gastrointestinal digestion of fish meat, because 
smoke phenolic components such as dihydroxybenzenes, 2,6-dimethoxy- and 2-
methoxy-phenols 
have 
proved 
antioxidant 
activity 
(Bortolomeazzi,

Sebastianutto, Toniolo, & Pizzariello, 2007; Huang, Chang, Sung, Vong, & 
Wang, 2011; Soldera, Sebastianutto, & Bortolomeazzi, 2008).  
Furthermore, it must be remembered that fish polyunsaturated omega-3 
lipids are especially prone to oxidation under digestive pro-oxidant conditions, 
which might impair their nutritional quality (loss of essential acyl groups) and 
safety (potential health detrimental effects of oxidation products) (Kristinova, 
Storrø, & Rustad, 2013; Larsson, Cavonius, Alminger, & Undeland, 2012; 
Larsson, Tullberg, Alminger, Havenaar, & Undeland, 2016; Steppeler, Haugen, 
Rodbotten, & Kirkhus, 2016; Tullberg et al., 2016). In fact, pioneer studies on 
the in vitro or in vivo gastric and/or duodenal digestion of oxidized turkey meat, 
myoglobin-added linoleic acid, fresh mullet (fatty fish), and beef-sunflower oil 
mixture reported a lower advance of lipid oxidation in the samples containing 
polyphenols than in the control ones; these polyphenols were either naturally 
present in red wine, grape seed extract, apple, plum and artichoke, or were added 
as pure standard compounds like resveratrol, epicatechin and caffeic acid 
(Gobert, Rémond, Loonis, Buffière, Santé-Lhoutellier, & Dufour, 2014; Gorelik 
et al., 2005; Gorelik, Ligumsky, Kohen, & Kanner, 2008; Kerem, Chetrit, 
Shoseyov, & Regev-Shoshani, 2006; Maestre, Douglass, Kodukula, Medina, & 
Storch, 2013). 
Nevertheless, it must be pointed out that in most of the above-mentioned 
digestion studies classical methodologies were employed for the analysis of lipid 
oxidation, such as measurement of the generation of hydroperoxides by peroxide 
value (PV) or ferrous ion oxidation-xylenol orange (FOX-2) assays, or 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 6 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
5 
 
measurement of the formation of malondialdehyde by the thiobarbituric acid 
reactive substances (TBARS) test. It is well-known that these classical 
methodologies are not able to provide either information about the specific nature 
of the lipid oxidation products generated or a real picture of the oxidation level of 
a sample; for instance, a sample with low hydroperoxide content can be either 
slightly oxidized or very oxidized, and TBARS test has been largely criticised 
due to its unspecificity (Frankel, 2005; Schaich, 2016). It is worth noting that 
Kerem et al. (2006) employed not only PV, but also an innovative technique that 
can provide a great deal of information, Solid Phase Microextraction followed by 
Gas Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (SPME-GS/MS); however, only 
hexanal abundances were determined in the headspace of the digests. This takes a 
very limited view of the oxidation process which occurs, because it is well-known 
that as many oxidation markers as possible should be considered in order to get a 
“real picture” of the complex lipid oxidation reactions taking place. In addition, it 
must be noted that most of the studies on the antioxidant activity of smoke 
phenolic compounds have been carried out using chemical assays, like radical 
scavenging assays using 2,2′-azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulphonic acid) 
(ABTS) and 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), whose drawbacks limit their 
usefulness in reflecting what takes place in in vivo or in real food systems (Prior, 
Wu, & Schaich, 2005). 
In a recent study carried out in our laboratory, the occurrence of lipid 
oxidation during in vitro digestion of farmed European sea bass meat was proved 
by means of 1H NMR and SPME-GC/MS (Nieva-Echevarría, Goicoechea,

--- Page 7 ---

Manzanos, & Guillén, 2017); moreover, it was evidenced that fish salting 
enhanced the advance of oxidation reactions under digestion conditions. In this 
context, and following this research line on the effect of common technological 
processes on the changes occurring in lipids during in vitro gastrointestinal 
digestion, the aim of this study is double. On the one hand, to evaluate the effect 
of the smoking process with two liquid smoke flavourings on lipid hydrolysis and 
oxidation occurring during in vitro gastrointestinal digestion of European sea bass 
(Dicentrarchus labrax). And on the other hand, to determine to what extent the 
type of flavouring selected may influence these reactions. For this purpose, 
innovative techniques like Proton Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (1H NMR) and 
SPME-GC/MS will be used, because they allow a global study of the samples in a 
simple way and without any previous chemical modification, as previously 
carried out in our laboratory (Vidal et al., 2016abc; Goicoechea, Brandon, 
Blokland, & Guillén, 2008; Goicoechea et al., 2011; Nieva-Echevarría, 
Goicoechea, Manzanos, & Guillén, 2014, 2016, 2017). This study sets out to 
provide a global view of how the mechanisms and extents of sea bass lipid 
hydrolysis and oxidation processes could be affected, if any, by the presence of 
smoke-derived compounds showing potential antioxidant activity. 
2. Materials and Methods 
2.1. Fish specimens 
Four specimens of farmed European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) were 
acquired from a local supplier within 48 h of harvest. The average body weight 
of the specimens was 1352.1±48.7 g. On the same day of purchase fishes were 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 8 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
7 
 
gutted, cleaned, filleted and skinned just before smoking. From each specimen, 
one fillet was maintained unprocessed as control (U) and the other fillet was 
submitted to smoking. The average weight of all the fillets was 240.3±13.1 g. 
The average molar percentages of the several kinds of acyl groups in European 
sea bass fillets, determined by 1H NMR (Vidal, Manzanos, Goicoechea, & 
Guillén, 2012), were the followings: 21.4±0.7% of saturated acyl groups and 
78.6±0.7% of total unsaturated acyl groups; the latter consisting of 41.8±0.7% of 
oleic (plus other minor unsaturated acyl groups), 22.5±0.7% of diunsaturated 
omega-6 (mainly linoleic), 14.2±0.6% of polyunsaturated omega-3 acyl groups, 
which include 5.8±0.3% of docosahexaenoic (DHA) and 5.1±0.4% of 
eicosapentaenoic (EPA), and 0.1±0.0% of omega-1 acyl groups.  
2.2. Liquid smoking procedure  
The liquid smoking procedure consisted in the immersion of the European 
sea bass fillet for 1 min in a solution of smoke flavouring in water (1:6, v/v) with 
a fish-to-flavouring solution proportion of 1:16 (w/v). Afterwards, smoked fillets 
were kept at room temperature for 2 h to facilitate the interaction between smoke 
components and fish flesh. In this study two commercial aqueous smoke 
flavourings (A and B) were used. Two fillets were smoked with flavouring A, 
named SA, and another two with flavouring B, named SB. These smoke 
flavourings A and B were selected because: i) they differ in their phenolic 
concentration (19 g/L and 24 g/L respectively, according to the manufacturer); ii) 
they have been employed in previous works carried out in our laboratory on 
oxidative stability and evolution during refrigerated storage of smoked European

--- Page 9 ---

sea bass and thus, their performance under these conditions is known (Vidal et 
al., 2016ab); and iii) the composition of the dichloromethane extracts of 
flavourings A and B is also known, having been studied in detail by GC/MS in 
the above-mentioned works. 
2.3. In vitro gastrointestinal digestion  
Immediately after carrying out the smoking process, in vitro digestion 
experiments were carried out. For this purpose, unsmoked and smoked European 
sea bass fillets were minced in a grinder and then, 4.5 g of each sample were in 
vitro digested following the gastrointestinal model developed by Versantvoort, 
Oomen, Van de Kamp, Rompelberg, & Sips (2005), slightly modified as 
described in detail before (Nieva-Echevarría, Goicoechea, Manzanos, & Guillén, 
2016). This model involves a three-step procedure which simulates digestive 
processes in the mouth, stomach and small intestine by adding sequentially the 
corresponding digestive juices. The transit times employed for oral, gastric and 
intestinal in vitro digestion were 5 min, 2 h and 4 h respectively. Digestive juices 
(saliva, gastric juice, duodenal juice and bile juice) were prepared artificially in 
accordance with the original model, although some modifications were 
performed in order to reach a higher level of lipolysis: addition of Aspergillus 
niger lipase to the gastric juice at 100 U/mL and decrease from 30.00 g/L to 
18.75 g/L of bovine bile extract concentration in the bile juice. All the reagents 
used were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA).  
For consistency of results, digestion experiments were performed in 
duplicate. Thus, the digests obtained from the in vitro digestion of unsmoked sea

bass were named DU (n=8) and those obtained from smoked sea bass samples 
using flavouring A were named DSA (n=4) and from flavouring B, DSB (n=4). In 
addition, blank samples, corresponding to juices submitted to in vitro digestion 
conditions in the absence of fish meat (J, n=4) were also analyzed.  
2.4. Fish lipid extraction and study by 1H NMR 
Lipids from European sea bass samples before (U, SA, SB) and after 
digestion (DU, DSA, DSB) were extracted with dichloromethane (CH2Cl2, 
Sigma-Aldrich), as in previous studies (Nieva-Echevarría et al., 2015, 2016, 
2017). This solvent was selected because of its ability to extract lipids, its high 
volatility and its suitable polarity. Before digestion, the lipids from minced fish 
muscle were extracted using dichloromethane in a proportion of 1:2 (w/v) and 
assisted by an ultrasonic bath for 1 h. After digestion, fish digests were 
submitted to a liquid-liquid extraction using dichloromethane in a proportion of 
2:3 (v/v). Afterwards, solvent was eliminated by means of a rotary evaporator 
under reduced pressure at room temperature, in order to avoid lipid oxidation.  
The 1H NMR spectra of the lipid extracts were recorded in duplicate on a 
Bruker Avance 400 spectrometer operating at 400 MHz. The sample preparation 
methodology, the acquisition parameters and the study of the spectral data were 
the same as those used in previous studies (Guillén & Ruiz, 2004; Vidal et al., 
2012). The relaxation delay and acquisition time allowed the complete relaxation 
of the protons, the signal areas thus being proportional to the number of protons 
that generate them, making their use for quantitative purposes possible. The 1H 
NMR spectra were plotted at a fixed value of absolute intensity to be valid for

2.5. Study by SPME-GC/MS of the headspace composition of the 
digests 
Solid Phase Microextraction (SPME). Extraction of the volatile 
components of the headspace of the several samples (0.5 g in 10 mL screw-cap 
vial) was performed in duplicate and carried out automatically using a 
CombiPAL autosampler (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), in 
agreement with previous studies (Nieva-Echevarría et al., 2017). Samples were 
the following: digestates obtained in the two digestion experiments from 
unprocessed sea bass (DU) and from smoked samples using flavourings A and B 
(DSA, DSB), together with the juices submitted to digestion conditions in the 
absence of fish (J); in addition, the headspace composition of fish fillets before 
digestion (U, SA, SB) was also analyzed. The fibre used was coated with 
Divinylbenzene/ Carboxen/ Polydimethylsiloxane (DVB/CAR/PDMS) (50/30 
μm film thickness, 1 cm long), acquired from Supelco (Sigma-Aldrich), which 
was inserted into the headspace of the sample and maintained for 60 min (50ºC).  
Gas Chromatography/Mass Spectrometry (GC/MS). The fibre containing 
the extracted components was desorbed for 10 min in the injection port (splitless 
mode with 5-min purge time) of a 7890A gas chromatograph equipped with a 
5975C inert mass selective detector MSD with Triple Axis Detector (Agilent 
Technologies) and a computer operating with the ChemStation program. The

operating conditions, and the identification and semiquantification of the 
headspace components were the same as in previous studies (Nieva-Echevarría et 
al., 2017).  
2.6. Statistical analysis 
The significance of the differences on the molar percentages of lipolytic 
products among samples and on the abundance of volatiles compounds detected 
in the digests was determined by one-way variance analysis (ANOVA) followed 
by post hoc Tukey b test or by t-Student test at 0.05 threshold, using the 
Statistical package SPSS v.22 (IBM, NY, USA). 
3. Results and Discussion 
3.1. Changes occurring during in vitro digestion in the lipids of 
unsmoked and smoked sea bass studied by 1H NMR 
3.1.1. Lypolysis extent 
Fish lipids are made up mainly of triglycerides (TG) and digestion provokes 
their hydrolysis to yield mainly 1,2-diglycerides (1,2-DG), 2-monoglycerides (2-
MG), fatty acids (FA) and glycerol. As can be observed in Table 1, before 
digestion, TG are the main components in unsmoked (U) and smoked (SA and 
SB) samples (see AGTG%). In addition, these three lipid extracts only contain a 
small proportion of FA (0.7-0.8%), DG and MG being absent. These results 
clearly indicate that the smoking process itself does not provoke sea bass lipid 
hydrolysis. This can also be directly deduced from the observation of 1H NMR 
spectra of U, SA and SB lipid extracts in Fig. 1, in which the specific signals of 
protons in the glycerol backbone of TG were the main ones (see the two doublets 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 14 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
13 
 
of doublets centered at 4.22 ppm and the multiplet at 5.27 ppm); by contrast, the 
proton signals related to partial glycerides were absent at 3.6-5.2 ppm. It must be 
noted that all these 1H NMR signals related to lipolytic products were described 
in detail before (Nieva-Echevarría et al., 2014,2015). 
As expected, the in vitro digestion process provoked the hydrolysis of both 
unsmoked and smoked sea bass lipids (see DU, DSA and DSB in Table 1). It is 
worth highlighting the high proportion of TG (≈94%) transformed into 1,2-DG, 
MG and glycerol, yielding a very high proportion of FA (≈64%). Moreover, in 
the three cases, it was evidenced that small amounts of 1-MG were generated due 
to the isomerization of 2-MG. The average molar percentage of the total chains 
that would be bioaccessible (this is to say AG2-MG%+AG1-MG%+FA%) is 
estimated to be ≈77% in either DU, DSA or DSB lipid extracts (p>0.05). 
Therefore, it was proved that smoking did not provoke any change in the lipid 
hydrolysis during sea bass meat in vitro digestion. Regarding this issue, it is 
worth mentioning that a previous study on in vitro digestion of salmon muscle 
and salmon oil reported a higher lipolysis level in the presence of phenolic 
compounds from a broccoli extract (Aarak, Kirkhus, Johansen, Vegarud, & 
Borge, 2014).  
Moreover, it must be pointed out that, in comparison with other in vitro 
studies (Larsson et al., 2012; Tullberg et al., 2016), a high degree of fish lipid 
hydrolysis, relatively close to that reported in vivo, has been reached during these 
digestion experiments. In fact, in humans, approximately 95% of triglycerides are 
absorbed as monoglycerides and fatty acids (Golding & Wooster, 2010).

These quantitative results can also be directly deduced by comparing the 
intensity of the specific proton signals due to TG, 1,2-DG, 2-MG and 1-MG that 
appear in the spectral region ranging from 3.5 to 5.3 ppm in DU, DSA, DSB 
spectra (see Fig. 1), in agreement with those previously described (Nieva-
Echevarría et al., 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017). The occurrence of considerable TG 
hydrolysis is also evidenced by the broadening and chemical shift displacement 
of the proton signals appearing from 2.25 to 2.45 ppm, due to the protons in 
alpha-position (and also in beta-position for docosahexaenoate) in relation to the 
carbonyl group of AG supported in glycerides and to the carboxyl group of FA 
(Nieva-Echevarría et al., 2014, 2015)  (see the enlarged spectral region in Fig. 1). 
3.1.2. Lipid oxidation extent  
Like any other lipid oxidation process, that of fish lipids involves the 
occurrence of several reactions that can give rise to a great variety of compounds. 
However, in comparison with that occurring in lipids of other animals or of 
vegetable origin, in marine lipids this oxidation process is expected to be one of 
the most complex ones, due to the high proportion of polyunsaturated acyl 
groups, showing up to six double bonds, which makes them especially prone to 
oxidation. In the classical scheme of this reaction, at initial stages primary 
oxidation compounds supporting conjugated double bonds and hydroperoxy 
groups are expected to be formed, later degrading into so-called secondary 
oxidation compounds, among which aldehydes can be cited. Nevertheless, both 
the evolution of the process and the specific nature of the generated compounds 
are greatly dependent on the oxidative conditions and on the nature and 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 16 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
15 
 
concentration of the lipidic substrates involved (Frankel, 2005; Martínez-Yusta, 
Goicoechea, & Guillén, 2014). By means of 1H NMR spectroscopy, the presence 
in a lipid sample of oxidation compounds of very different nature can be 
evidenced in a fast and simple way, by verifying the occurrence of non-
overlapped signals in certain spectral regions. This is the case of spectral regions 
ranging i) between 2.6-3.2 ppm, where proton signals due to epoxides appear; ii) 
between 5.9-6.7 ppm, where signals corresponding to protons of conjugated 
dienes are observable; and iii) between 9.2-10.0 ppm, where aldehydic proton 
signals are visible (Guillén & Ruiz, 2004; Martinez-Yusta et al., 2014). Fig. 1 
shows the enlargements of these regions of the 1H NMR spectra of the lipid 
extracts of unsmoked and smoked sea bass fillets before (U, SA, SB) and after 
digestion (DU, DSA, DSB).  
Unsmoked (U) and smoked (SA, SB) sea bass lipids before digestion. As 
expected because of the freshness of sea bass fillets, before digestion no signals 
related to lipid oxidation products were observed in any of the spectra of 
unsmoked and smoked fish lipid extracts (see U, SA and SB in Fig. 1). It must be 
noted that in SA and SB spectra signals near 6.40, 6.57 and at 6.75-6.85 ppm are 
visible, in agreement with a previous 1H NMR study of the oxidative stability of 
smoked sea bass samples (Vidal et al., 2016b). These signals are related to 
aromatic protons of phenolic compounds coming from the smoke flavourings, 
such as guaiacol, syringol, their alkyl-derivatives and other phenol derivatives 
that have been incorporated into sea bass fillets during the smoking procedure, as 
evidenced in a previous study on the headspace composition of both kinds of 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 17 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
16 
 
smoked sea bass fillets (Vidal et al., 2016a). The intensities of these 1H NMR 
signals due to phenolic compounds are slightly higher in SB than in SA spectra, 
indicating that sea bass fillets smoked using smoke flavouring B contain a higher 
phenolic content than those smoked using smoke flavouring A, in accordance 
with the phenolic concentration in each flavouring given by the manufacturer (24 
g/L and 19 g/L respectively).  
Digested unsmoked sea bass lipids (DU). After in vitro gastrointestinal 
digestion, new signals appeared in the spectrum of the lipid extracts of unsmoked 
sea bass digests (see DU in Fig. 1): signals a centered at 6.00 and 6.58 ppm due 
to protons of (Z,E)-conjugated dienes supported on chains having also a 
hydroperoxy group, and with much lower intensity, incipient signals b at 5.98 
and 6.48 ppm related to protons in (Z,E)-conjugated dienes supported on chains 
having also a hydroxy group (Gardner & Weisleder, 1972; Martínez-Yusta et al., 
2014; Murakami et al., 1992). Concerning the other two enlarged spectral regions 
shown in Fig. 1 at 2.6-3.2 and 9.2-10 ppm, no new signals were detected in DU 
spectrum. These results indicate that the extent of lipid oxidation taking place 
during in vitro digestion of unsmoked sea bass fillet is rather low, only yielding 
low amounts of primary oxidation compounds. This fact totally agrees with a 
previous study carried out on our laboratory addressing the effect of brine- and 
dry-salting processes on lipolysis and oxidation reactions affecting lipids and 
nitrogenated compounds taking place during in vitro digestion of farmed sea bass 
(Nieva-Echevarría et al., 2017). The estimated average concentration of (Z,E)-
conjugated dienic sytems supported on chains having also hydroperoxy or 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT

--- Page 18 ---

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
17 
 
hydroxy groups (Z,E-CD) in the lipid extracts of DU digests was 3.3±0.9 
mmol/molAG+FA. It must be noted that although many food studies measure 
hydroperoxides, because these are considered main oxidation markers, the 
formation of hydroxides under gastrointestinal conditions should also be taken 
into account. In fact, the generation of these latter has been widely reported in 
different biological systems, being considered by some authors as better 
biomarkers of in vivo oxidative stress than hydroperoxides (Niki et al., 2014).  
Digested smoked sea bass lipids (DSA, DSB). When comparing DU 
spectrum with those obtained from digested smoked sea bass lipids DSA and 
DSB, some differences are observed (see Fig. 1). One of them is that the above-
mentioned signals a and b appearing in DU spectrum, were not present in DSA 
and DSB spectra; hence, under the same simulated gastrointestinal conditions 
smoked sea bass lipids did not generate (Z,E)-conjugated dienes supported on 
chains having also hydroperoxy or hydroxy groups. This clearly points out that 
the smoking process provoked a clearly lower oxidation advance in the sea bass 
fillets during digestion, thus exerting some antioxidant activity. Another

4. Conclusions 
The present study demonstrates for the first time that smoking with liquid 
smoke flavourings, not only protects fish lipids towards oxidative conditions 
during storage, but also during gastrointestinal digestion. By means of 1H NMR, 
it was evidenced that smoking process does not affect the extent of lipolysis 
reaction during in vitro digestion of sea bass meat. By contrast, smoking using 
liquid smoke flavourings inhibits the generation of (Z,E)-conjugated dienic 
systems supported on chains having also hydroperoxy or hydroxy groups 
(primary oxidation compounds) that takes place during digestion of unsmoked 
fish samples. This protective effect of smoking towards sea bass lipid oxidation 
under gastrointestinal conditions was also confirmed by SPME-GC/MS. This 
highly sensitive technique was able to detect volatile secondary oxidation 
compounds present in concentrations below the limit of detection of 1H NMR. It 
showed, on the one hand, that the lowest abundances of volatile markers of 
polyunsaturated omega-3 and omega-6 lipids oxidation were found in the digests 
of smoked samples; and on the other hand, that the loss of the synthetic

hindered during digestion of smoked samples. This antioxidant effect of smoking

potential bioaccessibility of smoke flavouring components. This was proved by 
means of both 1H NMR and SPME-GC/MS. Among the smoke-derived

point of view since these compounds could also limit in vivo oxidative damage.
